How to check the mileage of a used VW, Audi, Seat or Škoda

Updated 12 November 2026

Plug a Bluetooth OBD adapter into the car and compare the odometer with the distance that other control units store (engine, gearbox, ABS and others) and with the mileage logged with each fault code. Units that agree support the reading, and a logged value above the odometer is a strong warning, but no result proves that a mileage is genuine.

Why the odometer alone is not enough

The number on the dashboard comes from one control unit, the instrument cluster, and it can be changed with tools that cost little. In a Volkswagen, Audi, Seat or Škoda the cluster is not the only unit that knows how far the car has driven. Several others keep a distance of their own in their measuring blocks, and many record the mileage at the moment they store a fault code. Each of those values is one more place that would have to be changed to hide a rollback.

A mileage check reads those values over the diagnostic socket and compares them with the odometer. It changes nothing in the car.

What you need

  • A Bluetooth ELM327 adapter that plugs into the car’s OBD socket. On Android, Classic Bluetooth and BLE adapters both work.
  • An Android phone with VAG Scope, or another tool that reads the control units of VW-group cars.
  • The seller’s permission, the ignition on and a healthy battery. The deep check reads every control unit for several minutes: if the voltage drops, start the engine briefly or connect a charger.
  • The value on the dashboard, in case the cluster does not answer.

Step by step

  1. Find the OBD socket, under the dashboard on the driver’s side, near the steering column or behind a small cover.
  2. Plug in the adapter, switch the ignition on and connect to the adapter from the app.
  3. Run the quick check. It reads the places where distances are most likely stored and takes about 30 seconds.
  4. If the result says there is not enough data, run the deep check. It searches every group of every control unit, takes a few minutes, and remembers where each unit keeps its distance so the next check is quick.
  5. If the cluster did not answer, type the value shown on the dashboard so the app has something to compare with.
  6. Read the result, then the evidence under it: each unit, the value it reported and whether it agrees.

How to read the result

ResultWhat it meansWhat to do
No discrepancy foundThe independent control units that answered agree with the odometer, within a tolerance of a few percent.Not a guarantee: several units can be corrected together. Still check the history.
No discrepancy found, limited evidenceOne unit besides the cluster agrees, backed by the mileages stored with fault codes.Weaker than a full agreement. Look for more evidence.
Some values do not fitSome stored values do not fit the odometer.Ask the seller, check the documents and have the car inspected before drawing conclusions.
Strong indication of a discrepancyStored values are clearly higher than the odometer shows.Treat the odometer with suspicion. Check documents and have the car inspected.
Data contradict each otherThe units contradict each other and the cluster.Nothing can be concluded from this check.
Not enough dataToo few units hold a mileage to compare with.Run the deep check, type the dashboard value, or rely on the documents.

The strongest sign: a mileage logged above today’s odometer

When a control unit stores a fault code, it often stores the mileage at that moment too. If the engine unit logged a fault at 182,000 km and the dashboard now shows 121,000 km, the car has travelled backwards, and that is a hard contradiction. Several independent units reading above the odometer is also a strong sign.

A unit that reads below the odometer is only a note. Control units get replaced and reset all the time, and a replacement starts counting from its own value.

Innocent reasons for a difference

  • Miles and kilometres. Some units only count in kilometres while the cluster shows miles. VAG Scope converts before comparing.
  • A replaced cluster. A new cluster is programmed with the old value, typed in steps of 10 km, and mistakes happen.
  • A unit from another car. An engine, gearbox or ABS unit taken from another car keeps the count of its donor. The VIN check shows which units came from another car.
  • Corrupted or saturated counters, for example exactly 655,350 km, or a negative or maximum value.
  • Tyre size or speed calibration. Units that add up speed over time can drift by a few percent.
  • Units that count differently: only while awake, reset by a software update, or holding a value that is not an odometer at all.
  • A wrong clock in the fault memory. Many units do not know the date, so dated readings can look implausible.

What the check cannot see

  • A professional correction of the cluster together with the engine unit and the gearbox.
  • Cars where only a few units answer (on some, just four) or where the units store no distance. Many control units from 2004–2010 do not store one at all.
  • A unit that only keeps a copy of the cluster value and was updated afterwards.

Agreement does not prove that an odometer is genuine, and a difference does not prove that anyone tampered with it. Use the result to ask better questions, never to accuse a seller.

Before you buy

  • Compare the result with the service history, invoices and inspection reports. Several countries keep official mileage records: the MOT history in the UK, HistoVec in France and Car-Pass in Belgium.
  • Look at the wear on the pedals, the driver’s seat and the steering wheel.
  • If anything does not fit, have the car inspected by an independent workshop before you pay.
  • If someone shows you a report, run the check yourself on the car in front of you: a report can be edited or come from another car. Why it matters.
